source_refs.note: Book p. 52: 2.10.1 definition of global (absolute) maximum and maximum value

blocks.text: Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) has a global (absolute) maximum at \(x = c \in I\), if \(f(c) \ge f(x)\) for all \(x \in I\).
If \(f(x)\) has a global (absolute) maximum at \(x = c\), then \(f(c)\) is called global (absolute) maximum value of the function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the definition as a competition: \(f(c)\) is compared with every value \(f(x)\) on the interval, and it is never beaten (it may tie). Then \(c\) is where the maximum occurs and \(f(c)\) is the maximum value.
The interval matters. On \([0, 2]\), \(f(x) = x^{2}\) has the global maximum value \(f(2) = 4\) (2.10.2, Example (a)); on \((-\infty, \infty)\) the same function has no global maximum at all, because its values grow without bound.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example: \(f(x) = 4 - x^{2}\) on \(I = (-\infty, \infty)\).
Since \(x^{2} \ge 0\), we get \(f(x) = 4 - x^{2} \le 4 = f(0)\) for all \(x\).
So \(f\) has a global (absolute) maximum at \(x = 0\), and the global maximum value is \(f(0) = 4\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Global maximum at \(c\): \(f(c) \ge f(x)\) for all \(x \in I\).
2. \(f(c)\) is the global maximum value; \(c\) is the point where it occurs.
3. The answer depends on the interval; a function may have no global maximum.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Giving only \(x = c\) when the question asks for the maximum value \(f(c)\), or the other way round.
2. Checking only a few values of \(x\): the inequality must hold for every \(x\) in the interval.
